Salt preserves by pulling water out of cells — microorganism cells as
much as vegetable cells. A 5% brine draws moisture across the membrane
until the osmolarity equalises, and at that point most spoilage
organisms can no longer multiply.

Water activity (aw) is the physical quantity underneath all of it:
how much of the water in a food is actually available to life. Sugar
lowers aw too, which is why jams keep without acid. Salt lowers it
more efficiently per gram. The two are interchangeable on the aw
scale, which is why sweet-and-sour preserves work.

The crispness of a fermented vegetable is the osmotic pressure
holding the cell walls taut — the trade-off with softness at high
salt is a balance, not a defect.
